records.author: cdce8p
records.body:
Building on the ideas from [PEP reference omitted] and after many discussions over the years, I’m happy to present PEP 824: None-coalescing operators. Please be sure to also check out the discussion for the companion PEP 823.

Abstract

This PEP proposes adding two new operators.

  • The “None-coalescing” operator ??
  • The “None-coalescing assignment” operator ??=

The general idea is to provide a conditional operator, similar to or, which instead of truthiness, checks for None values.

The “None-coalescing” operator evaluates the left-hand side, checks whether it is not None, and if not, returns the result. If the value is None, the right-hand side is evaluated and returned.

The “None-coalescing assignment” operator will only assign the right-hand side to the left-hand side if the left-hand side evaluates to None.

They are roughly equivalent to:

# a ?? b
_t if ((_t := a) is not None) else b

# a ??= b
if a is None:
    a = b

–
An interactive demo is available here: https://pep823-and-pep824-demo.pages.dev/

[PEP reference omitted]

[PEP reference omitted]

This PEP proposes adding two new operators.

records.author: effigies
records.body:
I would be very glad to see this accepted, and I am also glad to see it limited to exactly None. Extending to sentinels or other objects would replicate the pitfalls of __bool__.

Just a note on the precedence:

# x or y ?? 2
(x or y) ?? 2

# "Hello" if x ?? True else 0
"Hello" if (x ?? True) else 0

and

Furthermore, setting the precedence between or and conditional expressions matches other languages which have implemented the operator, like JS [PEP reference omitted] and C# [PEP reference omitted].

This is correct, but the JS and C# examples are interesting in that x || y ?? 2 is a type error in C# and a syntax error in JS. It may be worth exploring whether other languages permit intermixing with boolean operators, or if Python would be unique in this respect.

That said, I find the JS behavior surprising and annoying, so agree with the current design that parentheses should remain optional when precedence matches intent.

records.author: Boss_1s
records.body:
What if both Coalesce operators had their own dunder methods to change the check/assignment for None to something else like a custom Sentinel object? Would that be redundant or overly confusing?

Something like:

class Foo:
    MISSING = sentinel("MISSING")

    def __init__(self, bar=MISSING) -> None:
        self.bar = bar

    def __cgetattribute__(self, name, fallback): # ??
        # None-coalescing becomes MISSING-coalescing
        return fallback ?? self.name

    def __csetattr__(self, name, value): # ??=
        # None-coalescing assignment becomes MISSING-coalescing assignment
        if self.__cgetattribute__(self, name) is MISSING:
            super().__setattr__(name, value)

obj = Foo()

obj.bar ?? "unknown" # Returns "unknown"

obj.bar ??= "bax" # obj.bar is now "bax"
obj.bar ??= "baq" # obj.bar is still "bax"

obj.bar ?? "unknown" # Returns "bax"

(This example can be improved on)

records.author: cdce8p
records.body:
My bad. Almost all languages with coalescing operators use ?? and ??=. AFAIR all prior discussions, including PEP 505, used them as well.

Why ?? and not a single ?: The None-coalescing operator is a conditional operator. As such it’s more closely related to and / or than binary operators +, -, &, |, … Looking at other languages again, and is often spelled as &&, or as ||. Both use two chars to differentiate them from their binary counterparts.

records.author: steve.dower
records.body:
The ?? syntax has a very natural pairing with ?., and since they are two parts of what should usually be the same expression, it makes sense for both to have some level of consistency.[1]

By “natural pairing” I mean that a?.b ?? c should be a typical usage, where None is only really a special intermediate value and not an intentional result. Translated into current code, this would be a.b if a is not None and a.b is not None else c[2]. Both expressions are pretty good in this respect - the former uses punctuation operators and the latter using textual operators, and the precedence works as each naturally reads.[3]

  1. It’s irrelevant since I’ve withdrawn my own efforts on this, but I wouldn’t have split the PEP up into two. The value of ?? is strongest when ?. exists, and with either half of the syntax missing, the value quickly becomes zero or negative. ↩︎

  2. Without the repeated evaluations, of course. ↩︎

  3. Though, of course, I don’t prefer either syntax over a traversal helper function or a data model that simply doesn’t allow Nones to reach my business logic. ↩︎

records.author: hlovatt

For both @steve.dower’s and @pekkaklarck’s examples:

a?.b ?? c - I prefer the long form c if a is None or a.b is None else a.b

and

a ? b : c - I prefer the long form b if a else c

One of the things I like in Python is how readable it is, as opposed to how compact it is. I also am quite happy when Python doesn’t follow the crowd. I have used a ?? b in Swift, but the alternative is `a == nil ? b : a`

On the clear in preference to compact front, it is better to contain the nitty-gritty of parsing rather free-form input into a separate class or module so that the main logic remains visible and isn’t buried in None checks. Which further devalues a compact notion.

Would like Python to remain none computer scientist friendly.

records.author: steve.dower
records.body:
Nathaniel Sabanski:

Natural primitive for dynamic languages like Python where duck typing is prevailant and you very very often needing to ask for forgiveness, not permission.

Unfortunately (for your “strong +1”), this is not what the proposal does.

Duck typing does not naturally lead to the propagation of None in any way - they are entirely orthogonal. The concept of dealing with “members that may be None” is more likely to occur with a strict interface model, where you can’t get away with implementing “just enough” of an interface like you can in a duck-typing model like Python’s.

The proposal you seem to prefer would be the one that treats ?. as “get the attribute if the object has it, otherwise None” - this PEP (nor 823) is not that proposal. This is the one where the result of an operation is None and you want to break out of the current expression, which is neither a feature of duck-typing nor a likely outcome.

records.author: guido
records.body:
Looks like we’ve been side-tracked a little.

My reason for sponsoring both PEPs is that they replace common, verbose idioms with concise custom syntax.

Take a recent example,

c if a is None or a.b is None else a.b

Even with coloring, when you’re skimming code, this reads like

c if bla bla bla or bla bla bla else a.b

In the version using ‘?.’ and ‘??’, each name is used exactly once. In the if/else version, you have to carefully read the bla bla bla to confirm the correspondence of the variables and expressions to know what it does. This slows down reading, distracting the reader from comprehending the overall structure.

P.S. I don’t believe that Nathaniel wanted the interpretation that Steve assumed he wanted. His text is exactly the a?.b ?? c that Steve wanted earlier (and quoted at the top here).

records.author: guido
records.body:
Paul Moore:

The usual argument against “this is hard to understand” concerns is “people need to learn new features, and once they do, it’ll be fine”, which doesn’t seem to be happening here.

What you’re observing in this thread is multiple different people repeatedly getting the interpretation wrong. But there’s not much opportunity for learning this new feature by trying to use it – all we have is the PEP text. (And a demo sandbox, but I suspect very few people tried that before posting here.)

I also believe that your argument “people misunderstand it” is stronger in the PEP-823 thread (a?.b) than here (a ?? b). Once you learn about ?? it’s not hard to remember what it does: it does the same as or, which is already in widespread (ab)use for this idiom), except it checks whether the left operand is None instead of falsy. The None check is typically what people want, but often we are too lazy to write the whole if x is None thing.

For me, the strongest use cases for ?? and ??= are for function arguments whose type is T | None where None implies “use some other specific default”. For example, a function argument that should be a list shouldn’t be written as arg: list[T] = [].[1] But we can write it as arg: list[T] | None and then at the top of the function write arg ??= [].

The nice thing is that in this case a type checker will infer arg’s type as list[T] in the rest of the function body, so you don’t have to worry about shutting the type checker up about the None case, even though the argument has | None in its type.

And if you don’t use type checking, it still solves a real problem – mutable defaults are still evil so you still need to include

if arg is None:
    arg = []

Which I consider less readable than arg ??= [] because on first skim it reads as

if blah blah blah:
    blah = []

and now you have to read more carefully to confirm that it’s a None check and an assignment to the variable that’s None, before you can recognize the idiom for “use default if None”.

The use case for ?? is actually ever so slightly weaker – its’ most useful when arg is used only once in the function body (maybe being passed to another function). But it would be too weird to introduce ??= without ??.

  1. Mutable default ↩︎

records.author: guido
records.body:
I used AI to find the most contentious remaining issues in this thread, so I can try to address them all in one omnibus post (without quoting from individual messages – these are issues that were brought up repeatedly). In decreasing order of importance it listed:

  1. Whether PEP 824 is worthwhile independently of PEP 823
  2. Whether ??= earns its own syntax
  3. Why new syntax is justified at all
  4. Why ?? is preferable to a keyword spelling
  5. Whether the operator encourages excessive use of None
  6. Exact None semantics
  7. The relationship between the two PEPs7.
  8. Mixing with and and or

Going over the list:

1. Whether PEP 824 is worthwhile independently of PEP 823

I’m combining this with 7. The relationship between the two PEPs.

Perhaps PEP 505 shouldn’t have been split, but it’s a bit late to coalesce both new PEPs back into a single one. Ideally, both would be accepted, as they have some synergy. But either one by itself adds a significant new feature that can stand on its own (and opposition to 823 seems somewhat stronger than to 824). In my last post I pointed out the use case I expect to be using this most for, and that most definitely stands on its own. And note that, for example, C# introduced ?? in 2005 but ?. a declade later.

2. Whether ??= earns its own syntax

In my last post I mentioned that ??= is a stronger feature than ?? so I do think so.

3. Why new syntax is justified at all

My main argument (for both PEPs) is that the more traditional spelling using e.g. b if a is None else a reads as b if bla bla bla else a, which requires careful reading to confirm that bla bla bla actually checks whether a is None and not whether some other variable is None.

4. Why ?? is preferable to a keyword spelling

It’s the spelling in every other language that has this feature. While I’ve sometimes chosen to use keywords instead of conventional operators (last in 2006 for the if-expression) I used existing simple English words, not made-up neologisms like ifelse. And I’m sorry, Barry, but I find otherwise too long to type, and also it’s rather nonspecific about what it does. ifnone is more specific, but still asks the question “if what is None?”. In any case there wasn’t much support for either of these alternatives.

5. Whether the operator encourages excessive use of None

Steve Dower and Mike H have brought this up. Honestly I don’t yet understand their arguments, and have asked for a clarification. My current position is that optional components occur all the time in real life data and we must be able to deal with them efficiently.

6. Exact None semantics

This issue asks about configurability of the specific check that’s being executed to test whether to take the second branch or not. There hasn’t been much support for this proposal. It slows down the common case significantly – we’d need a new bytecode instruction that checks for None. This is cheap; but if the value is not None, it has to do an expensive method lookup to find the overridable dunder that implements the check, doing a lot of unnecessary work in the common case where no such dunder is defined. The cost of this would lead people to try to avoid the operator in favor of less precise approaches (notable going back to or).

7. The relationship between the two PEPs

Answered above with (1).

8. Mixing with and and or

This is the question about operator precedence. The PEP puts it above (grouping less tightly than) or. For example, a ?? b or c is read as a ?? (b or c), which makes some sense; also, a or b ?? c reads as (a or b) ?? c which I guess also makes sense.

The PEP puts it below if-else, so that e.g. a ?? b if c else d is read as (a ?? b) if c else d, which makes perhaps a little more sense than reading it as a ?? (b if c else d).

I don’t object to the PEP’s choices, but placement below not might also make sense. It feels pretty rare to combine ?? with the boolean operators anyway, and I might well parenthesize those cases. At the same time I don’t want to go the JavaScript way, which requires parenthesization in such cases.

There’s another, related issue – associativity, IOW what should a ?? b ?? c do. The PEP doesn’t say. It turns out that regardless of whether you evaluate it as (a ?? b) ?? c or a ?? (b ?? c), you always get the same outcome! (The first non-None value, if any.) But the former, (a ?? b) ?? c evaluates the outcome of a ?? b redundantly even if it is already not None, whereas a ?? (b ?? c) evaluates each at most once, from left to right. The spec implicitly indicates that a ?? b ?? c is a single chain of ?? operators, trying the operands one at a time, stopping at the first not-None value. So we might as well make this more explicit by saying (in the Precedence section) that the operator is considered right-associative. (I also suggest adding an example showing how a ?? b if c else d works.)

records.author: barry
records.body:
Guido van Rossum:

I used AI to find the most contentious remaining issues in this thread, so I can try to address them all in one omnibus post

I really appreciate your post, and I’ve been avoiding saying too much on the PEP 823/824 threads because I really don’t want to even hint at a bias given my (possible) role as one member of an SC that might decide their fates. That said, I’ve put a lot of thought into how I’ll approach deliberation on the PEPs if they are presented to the current SC for decision, which they haven’t yet been. That timeline is totally up to the PEP authors, so maybe I’ll just get to be a spectator when the time comes .

As an SC member, there’s no hiding the fact that I have personal opinions, but whether I lean for or against a PEP, I always try to ask myself “what’s best for Python?” I’m not special among my SC colleagues, all of whom truly do consider every nuance and angle from the same perspective. The wonderful thing about serving with such exceptional people is the way we help each other see past our individual biases, and look at the wider impact, long term view, and overall benefit.

Because the PEPs haven’t been submitted to the SC, we have not yet even discussed them[1]. I have no idea what my fellow SC members think about these PEPs.

So with that preamble, what follows are my personal thoughts.

Guido van Rossum:

opposition to 823 seems somewhat stronger than to 824

I think this is because 823 reads more like line noise than 824. One of the things that appealed to me so much about Python, oh 30+ years ago was how cleanly it read, especially as opposed to Perl. Python has been pretty true to that ideal over the years, but to me, 823 feels like a step backward. You can argue that long strings of ?. and ?[] won’t be common, but I’m not so sure. I think we won’t know until the feature is out there, with code bases that can floor on Python 3.16[2].

Especially as my eyes get older, it gets harder to pick out all the little squiggles and smudges which leads to the impression of line noise code. Maybe IDEs with their syntax highlighting and other assistances can help, and maybe in the world of agentic coding it won’t matter anyway, but I still like to read code, and I think 823 will make that harder. I don’t disagree with your blah blah blah observations, but complicated code is complicated. I don’t see how 823 helps readability, and it may make it worse.

Guido van Rossum:

In my last post I mentioned that ??= is a stronger feature than ?? so I do think so.

It could be, but to me, it’s also the more head-scratch inducing syntax. For a ??= b the PEP defines the semantics as “if a is None, assign b’s value to a”, but it could also incorrectly be interpreted as “assign b to a but only if b is not None”. I don’t think it’s immediately obvious at first glance and I don’t think it’s a slam dunk “learn it once, know it forever”. If the syntax is encountered infrequently, I worry that it’s just cognitively ambiguous enough to slow the reader down, making them have to reason out what it does and why the semantics are as the PEP specifies.

Guido van Rossum:

My main argument (for both PEPs) is that the more traditional spelling […] requires careful reading to confirm that bla bla bla actually checks whether a is None and not whether some other variable is None.

Perhaps, but [PEP reference omitted] is nearly 24 years old now, so we have a lot of experience with it. It’s terrible when you have a lot of nested if-else clauses, but that’s often a red flag that the code is trying to be too clever, where spelling it out might be tedious, but improves the readability. And I recall something that you said @guido when you were choosing this exact syntax over all the other alternatives. Paraphrasing[3] it was that you wanted a syntax that was just awkward enough to discourage its common use over plain 'ol if statements. If that’s true, you might not have succeeded .

Guido van Rossum:

It’s the spelling in every other language that has this feature. While I’ve sometimes chosen to use keywords instead of conventional operators (last in 2006 for the if-expression) I used existing simple English words, not made-up neologisms like ifelse. And I’m sorry, Barry, but I find otherwise too long to type, and also it’s rather nonspecific about what it does.

records.body:
Barry Warsaw:

I do think these PEPs elevate None to something even more special than it already is. With [PEP reference omitted] being introduced in Python 3.15, I wonder if that’s the path we really want to go down.

I don’t think there’s any obvious alternative Python could choose, but I also don’t think we box us in too bad with ??. The if x is None pattern is extremely common, ?? will be a great help, and this operator has proven itself in many other languages. Python differs from many other languages in that None appears as an ordinary object, but in all practical respects it’s equivalent to C# null, Perl undef, JS/TS null/undefined.

Personally, I’m very fond of custom sentinels and avoid using None in new APIs, but there’s no good way to extend a ?? operator to arbitrary sentinels.

  • Semantics like if isinstance(x, ANY_SENTINEL) would be wrong – when using sentinels we want to special-case only exactly that one sentinel by identity. In particular, custom sentinels are useful for being able to treat None as a normal value.
  • So a more general ?? version would require a way to specify the sentinel, which turns this into a ternary operator (value, sentinel, fallback). Such syntax may be possible (e.g. value ?? fallback could be a shorthand for something atrocious like value ??[None] fallback or value otherwise(None) fallback), but I don’t believe there can ever be agreement on such a syntax.

In practice, what I use instead is a sentinel-aware coalesce() function, something similar to this:

def coalesce[T, D, S = None](value: T|S, default: D, *, sentinel: S = None) -> T|D:
    if value is sentinel:
        return default
    return value

coalesce(value, default)  # value ?? default
coalesce(value, default, sentinel=MISSING)  # hypothetical ternary

If a None-only ?? operator proves popular and demand exists for custom sentinels, then it could perhaps make sense to add a dedicated method on the standard library sentinel type. E.g.:

MISSING = sentinel("MISSING")

MISSING.coalesce(value, default)  # default if value is MISSING else value

Not as convenient as a dedicated operator, but more convenient than an external function or than spelling out the conditional.

records.author: guido
records.body:
In the PEP 823 thread, Trey Hunner had an insightful question:

PEP 823: None-aware access operators

It would be nice to see much more detail in the “How to Teach This” section.

I replied there for PEP 823; here’s my corresponding proposal for PEP 824. Again, I’m happy to collaborate on improvements. (But we should leave some work for book/tutorial authors. )

How to Teach This

Basics

The ?? operator is a short-circuit operator like and and or that only checks whether its left argument is None. The others check for truthiness/falsiness, and treat values like 0, "", [] as falsy.

It is equivalent to a if a is not None else b. (Just like a or b is equivalent to a if a else b.)

Example: d.get(key) ?? make_default(key) is roughly equivalent to d.get(key, make_default(key)) except it only evaluate the default when needed. Also, it returns the default when d[key] returns None, while d.get(...) returns None in that case.

The ??= operator is the augmented assignment operator derived from ??. a ??= b means the same thing as a = a ?? b, except a is only evaluated once.

Chaining

An expression like a ?? b ?? c ?? d evaluates its sub-expressions (a, b, etc.) from left to right until it finds a value that’s not None or reaches the end.

Adding parentheses doesn’t change this – (a ?? b) ?? c has the same meaning as a ?? (b ?? c), since ?? is an associative operator (Google it :-).

Precedence

The ?? operator has a lower precedence than or and and. Thus, a or b ?? c means (a or b) ?? c and a ?? b and c means a ?? (b and c). To get the opposite grouping, use a or (b ?? c), etc.

However, this precedence is pretty arbitrary. As a style guide [maybe this could be added to PEP 8] we recommend always adding parentheses when mixing ?? with and or or.

When to use

This is useful when you find yourself writing things like a if a is not None else b a lot. The ??= operator is handy for providing defaults for arguments, like this:

def add_default_user(users: list[User] | None = None) -> list[User]:
    if users is None:
        users = []
    <manipulate users>
    return users

This can be compacted to

def add_default_user(users: list[User] | None = None) -> list[User]:
    users ??= []
    <manipulate users>
    return users

When not to use

Don’t use this when you also want to check for the other falsy values.

records.author: cdce8p
records.body:
Barry Warsaw:

It’s the “but slightly weaker” part that I think needs at least some discussion in the PEP.

My intuitive understanding here was that the more specialized a boolean operator is, the weaker its precedence needs to be for grouping to work as expected and ?? can basically be seen as a specialized version of or (however just for None). If-expressions are more specialized than and / or and ??. So the precedence should be even lower.

AI came up with this example, though I do think it illustrates the problem fairly well what would happen if the precedences for or and ?? were reversed:

The Real Breaking Case: user_name ?? default_name or "Guest"

Imagine you are fetching an optional configuration value.
• user_name could be None (missing), "" (explicitly cleared by user), or "Bob" (valid).
• If it is completely missing (None), you want to check default_name.
• If default_name is also empty or missing, you want to fall back to the string "Guest".
Let’s test this with user_name = "" (the user explicitly saved an empty string) and default_name = "Alice".

If or binds tighter than ?? (PEP 824 Proposal)

The expression is evaluated as: user_name ?? (default_name or "Guest")

  1. Python evaluates the left side: user_name is "".
  2. Because "" is not None, the ?? operator short-circuits.
  3. Result: "" (The user’s explicit empty string is preserved).

If ?? binds tighter than or

The expression is evaluated as: (user_name ?? default_name) or "Guest"

  1. Python evaluates the left group first: user_name ?? default_name.
  2. Since user_name is "" (which is not None), this group evaluates to "".
  3. Now, the remaining expression is: "" or "Guest".
  4. Because "" is falsy, the or operator triggers and moves to the right side.
  5. Result: "Guest"

And even the conclusion was spot on:

Why this breaks expectations

If ?? binds tighter than or, it destroys the ability to preserve falsy values (like "" or 0) earlier in the chain. The loose or at the end acts like a giant vacuum, overriding the strict None checks that happened to its left.

To keep the evaluation flowing strictly from left to right as an associative fallback chain, ?? must have a lower precedence than or. This ensures that any or operations finish grouping their truthy checks before ?? makes its final determination about whether the resulting value is strictly None.

records.author: guido
records.body:
Marc Mueller:

[Quoting AI]

To keep the evaluation flowing strictly from left to right as an associative fallback chain, ?? must have a lower precedence than or. This ensures that any or operations finish grouping their truthy checks before ?? makes its final determination about whether the resulting value is strictly None.

I’m not super convinced by the AI (it carefully picked an example where requiring or to bind tighter than ?? works out best), but it gave me an out-of-the-box idea.

There’s no reason that each operator should have a unique precedence – + and - have the same, as do * and / and //.

Since we appear to agree that ?? is a variant of or, why not give them the same priority? Then in a sequence of ?? and or operators the rule to follow is simply from left to right (just as it is for a sequence of just ?? or a sequence of just or) – the sequence will just return the first operand whose condition causes a shortcut to be taken. (Where the condition for a ?? b is a is not None and the condition for a or b is a, i.e., bool(a) != False.)

This leads to the same answer in the AI’s example, and feels easier to explain or to understand intuitively.

Are the two operators mutually associative? They are not: (a ?? b) or c does not always have the same outcome as a ?? (b or c), see the AI’s example. I’m not sure if that matters to anyone, but if it does, forget what I wrote.

records.author: Jelle
records.body: For what it’s worth I’d expect ?? to bind tighter than or. Punctuation feels like it keeps the operands closer together than a word does. It’s mostly true in Python today that operators that use punctuation bind tighter than those that use words: 6. Expressions — Python 3.15.2 documentation (with some exceptions, notably await and :=).

records.author: hprodh
records.body:
?? has a finer grain filtering than or, it only filters out the Nones.

Applying ?? after or will thus basically be useless, for example, in r = a or b ?? c, c will only be used if both a and b are None, thus the ?? is no more useful than or here.

Usually, one wants to replace specifically the None values first, and replace the falsy values afterwards.

The concept of “specialization” introduced above can be interpreted as a concept of “filtering thinness”.

records.author: cdce8p
records.body:
Guido van Rossum:

I’m not super convinced by the AI (it carefully picked an example where requiring or to bind tighter than ?? works out best)

Correct, it’s helpful to keep in mind though that in most cases there is actually no difference at all since both operators are associative and or handles None as well. What’s left is just the case the example highlighted: a ?? b or c where a is a falsy value but not None.

Looking at the example from another way, say ?? binds tighter, i.e. (user_name ?? default_name) or "Guest"

  1. For username = "" and default_name = "Alice"
  2. The group would evaluate to ""
  3. The remaining expression to "Guest" since "" is falsy

The default_name even though specified, would always be skipped. A tighter precedence breaks the fallback chain for any first falsy value other than None.

Guido van Rossum:

There’s no reason that each operator should have a unique precedence – + and - have the same, as do * and / and //.

That only works because addition and multiplication are commutative. a + b - c = a - c + b. For ?? the same precedence would actually work the same as having a stronger precedence than or (binding more tightly). That’s because (a or b) ?? c == a or (b ?? c) always evaluate the same since or handles None as well. So it’s only (a ?? b) or c and a ?? (b or c) which is different. The exact issue describe in the example above.

Let’s take a step back to look at how other programming languages handle it:

Language Precedence Implicit parsing behavior Requires grouping?
[PEP reference omitted] Weaker than or a ?? (b or c)
JS / TS Same tier as || Syntax error When mixing with && or ||
C# Weaker than || a ?? (b || c)
PHP Weaker than || a ?? (b || c)
Dart Weaker than || a ?? (b || c)
Swift Tighter than both && and || (a ?? b) || c
Kotlin Tighter than both && and || (a ?: b) || c

And in the context of the Python operator precedence:

Operator Description
.. ..
Swift, Kotlin
is, is not, … Comparisons, including identity tests
not x Boolean NOT
and Boolean AND
[1]
or Boolean OR
PEP 824, C#, PHP, Dart, (JS)
if - else Conditional expression

If we assume that ?? should be a boolean operator as it’s the case in the PEP, see the rejected idea [PEP reference omitted] for more details, a precedence that matches that of and and or more closely makes the most sense.

In practice, do I suspect developers will use something like a ?? b or c without parentheses, not sure, I probably wouldn’t. Can it be confusing though: sure, but thats’s what voluntary groupings and linter rules [2] are for, as suggested in the [PEP reference omitted] section.

  1. The alternative precedence we’ve been discussing above ↩︎

  2. I’d be surprised if RUF021 wouldn’t be updated to require parentheses for ?? as well if the PEP is accepted. ↩︎
